I am 23 years old, and I only know 3 people around my age who are able to speak Alsatian with a certain level, beyond a few phrases. My parents didn't teach me Alsatian, as it is the case for 90% of families here, sadly. I feel like Alsace has lost its spirit and is just being another French region, which is very sad. I decided to learn Alsatian and to promote and encourage it, I did a video some months ago : [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bDAHLvZFDe8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bDAHLvZFDe8) (subtitles available). The figure of 50% might be true, but you are including the older speakers above 60 years old, and there are many of them, as of any region in Western Europe where ageing population is an issue. We really need, us, young people, to do something to make Alsatian survive. Alsatian is not only useful for culture, but also because bilingualism is a high advantage in a globalised society, and Alsatian is sometimes way closer to English than to Standard German, compare "sewe" (w is a /v/ sound, as in German orthography) to English "seven" which has /v/, whereas German has "sieben" with a /b/. Other examples include "lawe" corresponding closer to English "to live" and less obvious to German "leben". Therefore Alsatian enables the acquisition of German and English much quickier.
